title: Diamonds
subtitle: A lock flight, a shrinking town, and a reservoir that has to last the year.
story: You are the new water master of a diamond town on the desert plateau. The diamonds lie in the beach gravels far below, and barges carry the gravel up a flight of locks to the washing plant. The annual river flood has just filled the reservoir at the top of the flight of locks, and it is the town's only fresh water until next year. This morning the season's first string of barges waits at the foot of the flight, and it has to reach the top before the evening fog closes in. Sail in to the gravel wharf, then climb the stairs and footbridges that zigzag up along the locks. As you go, do two things. First, analyze data from the town prospectors: they have surveyed new gravel pits along the old beach terraces. Use those data it to work out what determines whether a new pit will be rich in diamonds or not, and whether any of the new pits clear the threshold of being worth mining. Second, fill each lock to lift its barge, note what each fill  costs the reservoir, and pick up the lock-keepers' journal pages. At the gatehouse, work out how many more loads the reservoir can afford before the water runs short.

musicCredit.text: Majnoon — live at Rist Istanbul (Cafe De Anatolia)

escapeBrief: To get out you worked out how many more loads of gravel the town can bring up the locks before its water runs short. You are the water master, and the reservoir at the top of the flight is the town's only fresh water until the river floods again next year. It pays for two things: every lockful a barge uses on its way up, and whatever the town itself draws. You sailed in through the sea lock at the end of the breakwater, and its telltale board, which you could only read through the lock-keepers' telescope, showed it cost the reservoir 2 inches. Climbing the stairs beside the flight, you filled each of the five locks and watched its telltale show what it cost: 2, 3, 3, 3 and 4 inches. Six locks, 17 inches for every load. Pages from the lock-keepers' journals gave the town's drawdown for the last five dry seasons: 190, 166, 142, 118 and 106 inches, falling as people leave. On the drawdown board in the water master's office you set a peg on each season and released the rod. Its springs pulled it onto the straight line that sits closest to all five pegs, and it read about 80 inches for this season. The reservoir gauge read 360 inches after the flood, which leaves about 280 inches for the barges: 16 full loads, because 280 / 17 is 16.5 and half a load is no load. Averaging the past seasons gives 12, trusting last season alone gives 14, and forgetting the sea lock gives 18. The town is shrinking, so you needed the trend, which is exactly what fitting a line gives you, on the board or in R.

plannedHotspots.title: Penguins on a guano island
plannedHotspots.body: These are African penguins. They breed on Halifax Island, a stone's throw off the shore near Lüderitz. Their droppings, called guano, once lay deeper than a ten-story building is tall, and men were still digging the island for it in the years of this story. Today the African penguin is listed as Critically Endangered, one step from extinction. Almost all of them are gone, and the sardines and anchovies they hunt have nearly vanished from the waters around the island.

plannedHotspots.title: Diamonds delivered by a river
plannedHotspots.body: The diamonds in this gravel did not form on the coast. The Orange River carried them out of the African interior to the sea, and the waves, the wind and a current running along the shore then worked the river's cargo into diamond-rich beach gravels. hotspots.title: Diamonds delivered by a river
hotspots.body: The diamonds in this gravel did not form on the coast. The Orange River carried them out of the African interior to the sea, and the waves, the wind and a current running along the shore then worked the river's cargo into diamond-rich beach gravels. The rush began with a railway worker, Zacharias Lewala, who found a stone by the line and showed it to his supervisor. Soon the government closed almost the entire southern coast as the Sperrgebiet, the forbidden zone.

plannedHotspots.title: The beetles that drink the fog
plannedHotspots.body: These shiny black beetles drink the fog. They cannot fly, and they live only on the bare sand dunes of the Namib Desert. On foggy nights they climb to a dune crest, turn tail to the wind and stand on their heads. Fog gathers in droplets on their raised backs and runs down into their mouths. Of the related beetles scientists have compared, this is the only one that does the headstand.

hotspots.title: The beetles that drink the fog
hotspots.body: These shiny black beetles drink the fog. They cannot fly, and they live only on the bare sand dunes of the Namib Desert. On foggy nights they climb to a dune crest, turn tail to the wind and stand on their heads. Fog gathers in droplets on their raised backs and runs down into their mouths. Of the related beetles scientists have compared, this is the only one that does the headstand.

debrief.title: How this world worked
debrief.intro: This scenario was linear regression, fitting a straight line to measurements so you can see how much an outcome changes with each input, and then using that line to predict cases you have not measured yet. Here is what you did.

done.title: Barges for the gullies
done.body: The height line said climb high, and the two highest terraces looked like the richest claims. The whole survey says otherwise: the gravel that pays sits where the old shorelines cut gullies and potholes into the rock, and height only mattered because it travels with them. Pothole Bay and Shark Gully get the barges. The other half of the ruling is still waiting at the top of the flight: how many loads the water can afford.

escapeDone.title: The season's ruling
escapeDone.body: The town gate swings open and you climb out of the fog into clear sun. Below you the barges sit in their chambers, one to a lock, and the reservoir lies still behind the dam. Sixteen loads, to the two claims that pay: that is the ruling. It will not save the town for ever, but it gives the washing plant its season, and the families who stayed a reason to stay one more year.

coverPrompt: Minimalist stylised thumbnail poster, seen square-on and flat: the black silhouette of a stepped flight of canal locks climbing a desert slope from the lower left to the upper right, one low gravel barge in the top lock, set against a band of cold grey fog below and a single warm amber sky above, with one small bright glint on the barge's gravel. Bold, graphic, very few elements, high contrast, poster-like. No people, no text, no lettering, no letters, no numbers, no border.

ladderPlain.text: In the first puzzle you fit a straight line of claim grade against terrace height and read its slope: each extra meter of height went with about one more carat per hundred tons.
In the second puzzle you used that height line to predict the grade of a claim nobody had washed yet, Red_Sky, and it came out under the pay line.
In the third puzzle you scaled all six measurements, fit them together and compared their coefficients: gullies per hundred meters had by far the largest effect, and terrace height came fourth.

In the final puzzle you predicted all eight new claims from the six-measurement model, and Pothole_Bay and Shark_Gully were the two over the pay line, while the height line alone pointed to Eagle_Terrace and Summit_Beach, the two highest terraces, which all six measurements together rate among the poorest.
To get out you fit a straight line through five dry seasons of the town's water use, read this season's draw from it, and worked out that the reservoir could afford sixteen more loads.

worldPlatePrompt: A wide, high oblique aerial photograph from a light aircraft over a cold fog-desert coast in the 1920s, like the Namib's diamond coast near Luderitz. In the near ground the cold grey-blue Atlantic with low flat shelves of dark rock; a small walled harbour basin closed off by a long low rubble breakwater, with a small stone sea lock and its keeper's hut at its far end tight under a sheer rock headland; a gravel wharf with low gravel barges on the near shore of the basin. From the basin a stone-walled canal climbs straight inland as a flight of five locks, each a long stone chamber with timber gates, one step higher than the last, a gravel barge in each chamber; a timber footbridge on the lower gates of every lock and a stone stair beside the next lock, so the walking route zigzags up the flight. Down the right-hand hillside run five separate iron feed pipes, fanned apart, each from the dam to its own lock. At the top a stone dam holds a broad still reservoir, with a small stone gatehouse and a tall gauge post on the dam and a water master's office beside it; to the left on the plateau a half-abandoned diamond town of grand gabled houses in faded pastel plaster with corrugated-iron roofs, sand drifting into the doorways, and a stone town gate where the dam meets the town. Palette: pale apricot and cream sand, grey-brown rock, bone-white bleached timber, rust-red iron, faded pastel plaster, cold grey-blue water. Fog lies thick at sea and low over the basin, thinning level by level up the flight, the town in clear light above it. Soft even daylight. No people in close-up, no text, no labels, no modern machinery, no palm trees, no red rock.
